text:
A U.S. court found Google's search business a monopoly because it violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act by engaging in exclusionary conduct through default-distribution deals [Source: ev-1]. Judge Amit Mehta ruled on August 5, 2024, that these practices allowed Google to maintain its dominance in general search services and text advertising [Source: ev-1]. The core theory of harm was that Google paid billions of dollars to companies like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to be their default search engine; for instance, CEO Sundar Pichai testified that Google spent approximately $26.3 billion on distribution in 2021, and trial evidence indicated Google paid Apple roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue [Source: ev-1]. This created a self-reinforcing loop where paying for defaults generated scale, which led to more data, improved quality, and protected the default status against rivals [Source: ev-1].

On August 5, 20 has ordered structural remedies requiring Google to divest its Chrome browser—a move described as the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case in 2000—and prohibiting it from paying for default search placement through revenue-sharing agreements [Source: ev-1]. Additionally, the court imposed limits on Google's acquisitions and AI-related investments [Source: ev-1]. Although Google appealed this decision to the DC Circuit Court of Appeals in 2025, arguing that the ruling punished procompetitive innovation, the final outcome remained pending throughout 2025 [Source: ev-1].
